teile.einleitung: Air pressure is the force with which the air presses on everything around it. Above us there is a layer of air many kilometres high, whose weight is constantly pressing on us without our feeling it. When you blow air into a balloon, the air inside presses on the skin of the balloon, and the balloon gets bigger.
wichtigste: Air pressure comes from the weight of the air above us.
At sea level, air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.
The higher you go, the lower the air pressure becomes.
If you blow air into a balloon, the pressure inside rises and the balloon expands.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer.
High and low pressure areas determine our weather.
On high mountains, water boils below 100 degrees.

abschnitte.text: Air consists of countless tiny particles that are constantly flying about and bumping into everything. Air also has weight, even though it is light. So the whole layer of air above us presses on the Earth and on our bodies; this is **air pressure**. We do not feel it, because there is an equally strong counter-pressure inside our bodies. If you blow air into a **balloon**, there are more air particles inside pressing against the skin, and the balloon expands.

Air pressure is measured with a **barometer**. The first barometer was built by the Italian Evangelista Torricelli in 1643, using a glass tube full of mercury. Today air pressure is usually given in **hectopascals**, abbreviated hPa. At sea level it averages about 1013 hectopascals. That is roughly the weight of 10 tonnes on every square metre.

The higher you climb, the less air there is above you, and the air pressure falls. On the Jungfraujoch, at about 3450 metres, it is only about two thirds as high as at sea level. That is why you get out of breath more quickly there when climbing stairs. On high mountains, water boils below 100 degrees; at 3000 metres, for example, it boils at about 90 degrees. When you go up in a cable car, your ears “pop” because the pressure in your ear adjusts to the pressure outside.

Air pressure is not the same everywhere and is constantly changing. In a **high pressure area**, air sinks and the weather is usually fine and dry. In a **low pressure area**, air rises, clouds form and it often rains. The air flows from the high to the low, and this creates wind. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss measure air pressure in many places in order to forecast the weather.

In 1654 the mayor of Magdeburg, Otto von Guericke, showed the force of air pressure with a spectacular experiment. He put two metal hemispheres together and pumped out the air between them. After that, even several teams of horses could not pull the **Magdeburg hemispheres** apart. The air pressure from outside held them together. Suction cups that stick to smooth tiles use the same principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring instrument for air pressure.
The unit in which air pressure is usually given, hPa for short.
A zone of high air pressure, which usually brings fine weather.
A zone of low air pressure, which often brings clouds and rain.

gewusst: Air pressure puts a weight of several tonnes on a child, which the child does not notice at all because of the counter-pressure in the body.
Because air pressure is low at great heights, aircraft cabins are pressurised artificially.
A sealed bag of crisps can become really puffed up on a high mountain pass, because the air pressure outside is lower.

teile.einleitung: Margaret Mead was an American anthropologist, a researcher who studies the lives of people in different cultures. In the 1920s and 1930s she travelled to islands in the Pacific and wanted to find out how culture shapes the way children and young people grow up. She became one of the best-known scientists of her time.
wichtigste: Margaret Mead lived from 1901 to 1978.
She studied at Columbia University under Franz Boas.
In 1925 and 1926 she did research on Samoa for the first time.
Among the Manus people of the Admiralty Islands she studied childhood and returned decades later.
For decades she worked as a curator at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.
With the anthropologist Gregory Bateson, her husband, she did research on Bali.
In 1983 Derek Freeman sharply criticised her Samoa study.
In 1979, after her death, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

abschnitte.text: Margaret Mead was born in Philadelphia in the USA in 1901. Her parents were both teachers and researchers, which encouraged her curiosity early on. At Columbia University in New York she studied **anthropology** under Franz Boas, one of the founders of the subject. The anthropologist Ruth Benedict was also her teacher and became a close friend. Mead belongs to the so-called **culture and personality school**, which studied how a culture shapes people's character.

At only 23, Mead travelled alone to the island group of **Samoa** in the Pacific. There, in 1925 and 1926, she lived in villages for several months and watched how girls and young women grow up. She wanted to show that the teenage years are not equally difficult everywhere, but depend strongly on the culture. Her book about it was published in 1928 and became a bestseller. This made anthropology known to the general public.

Later Mead did research in New Guinea, today Papua New Guinea. Among the **Manus** of the Admiralty Islands she watched how children play and learn. Decades later she went back and saw how much life there had changed. With her husband Gregory Bateson she did research on **Bali** in the 1930s. The two took thousands of photos and film recordings, which was new in research at the time.

From 1926 Mead worked for decades at the **American Museum of Natural History** in New York, in the end as a curator. She wrote many books, gave lectures and spoke out in magazines and on television. She talked about family, upbringing, the environment and how different cultures live together. Many people saw her as a kind of explainer of the world. She died in New York in 1978.

Five years after her death, in 1983, the anthropologist **Derek Freeman** published a sharp criticism of her Samoa study. He claimed that Mead had misunderstood the Samoans and had jumped to conclusions too quickly. This led to a long dispute among experts that has still not been fully settled. What is undisputed is that Mead made fieldwork well known and paved the way into science for many women. In 1979, after her death, she received the **Presidential Medal of Freedom**, one of the highest honours in the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of human beings and their cultures.
Research in which you live among the people yourself and observe them.
An expert in a museum who looks after collections and plans exhibitions.
Everything a group of people has in common, such as language, customs and rules.

gewusst: On her travels Margaret Mead often carried a tall forked walking stick, which became her trademark.
Her daughter Mary Catherine Bateson also became an anthropologist.
For her research Mead always learned the language of the people she lived with.

teile.einleitung: The Manhattan Project was a secret research programme of the USA during the Second World War, in which the first atomic bombs were built. Thousands of researchers, technicians and workers took part in it. The consequences of this project still shape the world today.
wichtigste: The Manhattan Project ran from 1942 to 1946 in the USA, with support from Great Britain and Canada.
The military head was General Leslie Groves, and the scientific head at Los Alamos was J. Robert Oppenheimer.
One trigger was the Einstein-Szilárd letter of 1939 to President Roosevelt.
In 1942 in Chicago, under Enrico Fermi, the first controlled nuclear chain reaction succeeded.
On 16 July 1945 the first atomic bomb exploded in the Trinity test in New Mexico.
In August 1945 atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
By 1945 the project had cost about 2 billion US dollars.

abschnitte.text: At the end of 1938, **nuclear fission**, which releases huge amounts of energy, was discovered in Berlin. Many researchers feared that Nazi Germany could build a weapon from it. In 1939 Leó Szilárd, together with Albert Einstein, wrote a letter to US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, the **Einstein-Szilárd letter**. It is considered one trigger for the American atomic programme, which from 1942 ran under the code name Manhattan Project.

Overall military command lay with General **Leslie Groves**. He chose the physicist **J. Robert Oppenheimer** as scientific director of the new laboratory at Los Alamos in the state of New Mexico. Many of the best-known physicists of the time worked there, including refugees from Europe. At its height, well over 100,000 people worked on the project in total, but most of them did not know what they were working on.

On 2 December 1942, under the leadership of **Enrico Fermi** in Chicago, the first controlled nuclear **chain reaction** succeeded. The reactor was made of graphite blocks and uranium and stood under a stand at one of the university's sports grounds. This proved that nuclear energy can be released in a controlled way. This experiment is also considered the birth of nuclear power stations.

The project had several large, secret sites. At **Oak Ridge** in Tennessee, uranium was enriched, meaning the share of fissile uranium-235 was increased. At **Hanford** in the state of Washington, plutonium was produced in reactors. At Los Alamos the bombs were developed. Whole towns were built for this within a few months.

On 16 July 1945, in the desert of New Mexico, the researchers set off the world's first atomic bomb; the test was called **Trinity**. On 6 August 1945 the US Air Force dropped the uranium bomb “Little Boy” on **Hiroshima**, and on 9 August a plutonium bomb on **Nagasaki**. Tens of thousands of people died at once, and many more later from injuries and radiation damage. Shortly afterwards Japan surrendered, and the Second World War ended.

After the war, an **arms race** began between the USA and the Soviet Union, which also tested an atomic bomb in 1949. Many of those involved, including Oppenheimer, later warned of the dangers of nuclear weapons. Today there are international treaties meant to limit the spread of nuclear weapons. The cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki remember the victims with memorials and campaign for a world without nuclear weapons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases a great deal of energy.
A process in which each nuclear fission sets off further fissions.
The fissile form of the element uranium, used in atomic bombs and nuclear power stations.
A process that increases the share of uranium-235 in uranium.
A fissile element produced artificially in reactors.

gewusst: The name “Manhattan Project” comes from an army department that was based in Manhattan in New York at the start.
Officially the town of Los Alamos did not exist at all; post for researchers went to a post office box in Santa Fe.
The life of J. Robert Oppenheimer was told in the 2023 film “Oppenheimer”.

teile.einleitung: Marie Curie was a Polish-French physicist and chemist and one of the most famous researchers of all time. She was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, and together with her husband Pierre Curie she discovered the elements radium and polonium. She is the only person to have received Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences.
wichtigste: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867 and died in France in 1934.
In 1903 she was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, in physics.
In 1911 she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry.
With Pierre Curie she discovered the elements radium and polonium in 1898.
She researched radioactivity and coined this term.
She was the first woman professor at the famous Sorbonne in Paris.
She died from the effects of the radiation she had worked with for years.

abschnitte.text: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw on 7 November 1867 as **Maria Skłodowska**. At that time Poland belonged to the Russian Empire, and women were not allowed to study at university there. Maria was an excellent pupil and first worked as a governess to save money. In 1891 she moved to Paris and studied physics and mathematics at the **Sorbonne**. There she met the physicist Pierre Curie, whom she married in 1895.

The physicist Henri Becquerel had discovered that uranium gives off invisible radiation. Marie Curie studied this radiation more closely and called the phenomenon **radioactivity**. Together with Pierre she found two new chemical elements in 1898. She named the first **polonium**, after her home country Poland. She named the second **radium**, after the Latin word for ray, because it glows and radiates strongly.

In 1903 Marie Curie, Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel jointly received the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. Marie was thus the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. In 1906 Pierre died in an accident with a horse-drawn cart in Paris. Marie took over his professorship and so became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own for obtaining pure radium.

In the First World War, Marie Curie worked to help wounded soldiers. She had cars fitted with **X-ray machines**, which drove to the front. With these mobile X-ray stations, which were called “little Curies”, doctors could find bullets and broken bones in the body. Marie Curie went along herself and trained women as X-ray assistants. In this way she helped to save many lives.

At that time people did not yet know how dangerous radioactive radiation is. Marie Curie often carried radium in the pocket of her lab coat and became ill from the radiation. She died on 4 July 1934 in a sanatorium in the French Alps. Her daughter **Irène Joliot-Curie** also received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935. Today the chemical element curium is named after the Curies, and Marie's grave is in the Panthéon in Paris.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of some substances of giving off invisible, high-energy radiation by themselves.
A basic substance that consists of only one kind of atom, such as radium or oxygen.
One of the most important awards in the world for science, literature and peace.
A machine with which you can look inside the body, for example at bones.

gewusst: Marie Curie's notebooks are still so radioactive today that they are kept in lead boxes.
The Curie family won five Nobel Prizes in total, if you add together those of Marie, Pierre, their daughter Irène and their son-in-law Frédéric.
Marie Curie was the first woman to be buried in the Panthéon in Paris for her own achievements.

teile.einleitung: The dandelion is one of the best-known meadow flowers in Switzerland. In spring it turns whole meadows bright yellow, and later the flower becomes the fluffy dandelion clock. It gets its name from its jagged leaves, which look like lion's teeth.
wichtigste: The dandelion grows in meadows, pastures, by paths and in gardens.
Its leaves are jagged like teeth, which is where its name comes from.
If you break the stem, a white milky sap comes out.
The flower closes in the evening and when it rains.
It has a long, deep taproot and is hard to pull out completely.
Young dandelion leaves can be eaten as salad.
Rabbits especially like to eat dandelion leaves.

abschnitte.text: The dandelion forms a flat **rosette of leaves** close to the ground. From its centre grow hollow stems, each with one yellow flower head on top. What looks like a single flower is in fact made of many small **ray florets**, often well over a hundred. That is why the dandelion belongs to the **daisy family**, like the sunflower and the daisy.

After flowering, the flower head closes and opens again a few days later as a white ball. This **dandelion clock** is made of many fruits, each hanging from a fine little parachute of hairs. The wind carries the fruits far away like little parachutes. In this way the dandelion spreads very successfully to new areas.

A white, bitter **milky sap** flows in all parts of the plant. It makes stains on clothes that are hard to get out. Underground, the dandelion has a long **taproot** that reaches deep into the soil. If a piece of it stays in the ground when you pull it up, a new plant grows from it. Rubber can even be obtained from the milky sap of a related species.

Young dandelion leaves taste slightly bitter and are eaten as salad in spring. The flowers can be boiled with sugar into a sweet syrup, which some people call dandelion honey. In the past the roasted root was used as a coffee substitute. In folk medicine the dandelion is considered a remedy for digestion and the gall bladder.

In spring the dandelion is an important source of food for **bees**, bumblebees and butterflies. It provides plenty of nectar and pollen when little else is flowering yet. Rabbits, guinea pigs and tortoises love to eat its leaves. For farmers it is good fodder for cows, as long as it does not take over too much.

The dandelion's flowers open in the morning and close in the evening. They also stay closed in rain and dull weather. In this way the plant protects its pollen from getting wet. In Switzerland in April and May you often see whole **dandelion meadows**, especially on well-fertilised pastures.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family whose flower heads are made of many small single flowers.
A long, strong main root that grows straight down into the ground.
Leaves spread out in a circle on the ground.
A white liquid that flows in some plants.

gewusst: The name dandelion comes from the French dent-de-lion, which means lion's tooth.
A single dandelion clock can carry over a hundred fruits with parachutes.
Researchers are studying the Russian dandelion because rubber for car tyres can be made from its milky sap.

teile.einleitung: Maggi is a well-known brand of soups, stock and seasoning that started in Switzerland. It was founded by Julius Maggi from Thurgau, who in the 19th century wanted to develop cheap and nourishing ready-made food for working families. Many people still know the brown bottle of Maggi seasoning today.
wichtigste: Julius Maggi was born in Frauenfeld in 1846.
His factory was in Kemptthal near Winterthur.
He made his first ready-made soups from pea and bean flour.
In 1886 he invented a liquid seasoning, Maggi seasoning.
Around 1908 the Maggi stock cube came onto the market.
With hot water, a stock cube quickly becomes soup.
Since 1947 Maggi has belonged to the food company Nestlé.

abschnitte.text: Julius Maggi was born in 1846 in **Frauenfeld** in the canton of Thurgau. His father came from Italy and later ran a mill in Kemptthal. Julius took over the mill, but the flour business went badly. So he looked for new products. He died in 1912 and left behind a company that was active in many countries.

In the 19th century many people worked long hours in factories and had little time to cook. The factory inspector Fridolin Schuler campaigned for better food for working families. Together with him, from 1884 Maggi developed a flour made from **pulses**, meaning peas and beans. Nourishing, protein-rich soups could be cooked from it quickly. This was one of the very first **ready-made soups**.

To make his soups taste better, Julius Maggi invented a liquid seasoning in 1886. It went on sale in a typical brown bottle with a yellow and red label. Around 1908 came the **stock cube**, a pressed cube of salt, fat and spices. If you add hot water, you get stock in a few minutes. Such cubes were practical because they keep for a long time and are easy to carry.

The factory in **Kemptthal** near Winterthur became a large industrial plant with its own railway station. As early as 1887 Maggi also opened a factory in Singen in Germany, where the brand became especially popular. In 1947 the company merged with **Nestlé**. Today the old factory site in Kemptthal is used for businesses and homes. Maggi products are now sold in many countries, for example in Germany, Africa and Asia.

Ready-made soups and stock are practical when you need something quickly. But they often contain a lot of **salt**, so you should not use them too often. Home-made soups from fresh vegetables are usually healthier. Even so, many cooks use stock as a base for risotto, sauces or soups. In this way Julius Maggi's idea lives on in many kitchens.

begriffe.erklaerung: A clear, strong broth used as a soup or as a base for cooking.
Seeds of plants such as peas, beans and lentils, which contain a lot of protein.
A substance that gives food more flavour.
A soup that is already prepared and only needs to be cooked with water.

gewusst: The herb lovage is often called “Maggi herb” in German because it smells similar, even though Maggi seasoning contains no lovage at all.
The shape of the Maggi seasoning bottle has stayed almost the same for over a hundred years.
For a time, Maggi worked on his advertising with Frank Wedekind, who later became a famous writer.

teile.einleitung: Lucy is the nickname of a famous fossil, the skeleton of an early prehuman about 3.2 million years old. It was found in Ethiopia in 1974 and belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis. Lucy shows that our ancestors walked upright long before their brains became large.
wichtigste: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in East Africa in 1974.
She belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis.
The skeleton is about 3.2 million years old.
The research team was led by Donald Johanson.
She got her name from a Beatles song.
Lucy was about 1.1 metres tall and walked upright on two legs.
In Ethiopia she is called Dinkinesh.

abschnitte.text: Lucy was a female **prehuman** who lived about 3.2 million years ago. She belonged to the species **Australopithecus afarensis**, which means something like “southern ape from Afar”. Lucy was not a human like us, but not an ape either; she was a being somewhere in between. She was about 1.1 metres tall and weighed about as much as a schoolchild today.

On 24 November 1974, researchers near **Hadar** in the Afar region of Ethiopia discovered a bone on a slope. The team led by the American **Donald Johanson** then found many more parts of the same skeleton. Altogether about 40 per cent of the skeleton has survived, a sensation for such an old fossil. On the evening of the find, a Beatles song with the name Lucy in the title was playing in the camp, and so the skeleton got its nickname.

Lucy's pelvis and leg bones clearly show that she walked **upright** on two legs. Her brain, on the other hand, was only about as big as a chimpanzee's. This was an important discovery, because it shows that walking upright developed earlier than the large brain. Her long arms suggest that she could probably still climb trees well too.

In Ethiopia Lucy bears the name **Dinkinesh**, which means “you are marvellous” in Amharic. The real bones are kept in the National Museum in **Addis Ababa**. Visitors there usually see an exact replica, because the original is very fragile. For many people in Ethiopia, Lucy is a source of national pride.

For a long time Lucy was the oldest almost complete skeleton of a prehuman. She helped people understand that the cradle of humankind lies in **Africa**. Later more fossils of the same species were found, such as the skeleton of a child that researchers called Selam. Fossilised footprints from Tanzania also show that such prehumans walked upright.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from long ago that has turned to stone.
An early relative of humans who lived millions of years ago.
A genus of prehumans who lived in Africa about 4 to 2 million years ago.
Moving on two legs with the body held upright.

gewusst: Lucy was so famous that her bones were shown on an exhibition tour of the USA from 2007 to 2013.
A NASA space probe that flies to asteroids was named after Lucy.

teile.einleitung: A magnifying glass is a simple glass that makes small things look bigger. With it you can look closely at an ant, the veins of a leaf or the fine lines of a fingerprint. It is one of the oldest optical aids in the world.
wichtigste: A magnifying glass makes things look a little bigger.
It consists of a curved lens made of glass or plastic.
This lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge and is called a converging lens.
Magnifying glasses usually magnify about 2 to 10 times.
For stronger magnification you need a microscope.
A magnifying glass can focus sunlight and so start a fire.
Watchmakers often work with a magnifying glass in their eye.

abschnitte.text: A **magnifying glass** is a lens made of glass or clear plastic, often with a handle or in a frame. The lens bulges outwards, so it is thicker in the middle than at the edge. Such a lens is called a **converging lens**. If you hold it close to an object, the object appears bigger. Magnifying glasses usually magnify about two to ten times.

Rays of light are bent when they pass through the curved lens; we say they are **refracted**. As a result, our eye sees a magnified image of the object. The magnifying glass works best when the object is a little closer than the **focal point** of the lens. The more strongly curved the lens is, the more it magnifies. But then the image is often blurred at the edges.

A magnifying glass collects the Sun's rays in a small, bright spot, the focal point. It gets so hot there that paper or dry grass can start to burn. That is why a converging lens is also called a burning glass. You must never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass, because this can seriously injure your eyes. Even a magnifying glass left lying in the sun can start a fire.

As early as ancient times, people knew that curved glass or glass balls filled with water make things look bigger. In the Middle Ages, monks used so-called **reading stones**, hemispherical stones made of glass or rock crystal, which they laid on books. Spectacles, the telescope and the microscope later developed from such lenses. The magnifying glass also became the trademark of detectives such as Sherlock Holmes. To this day it is a symbol of looking closely and searching.

Many people use a **reading magnifier** to read small print. In the Swiss **watch industry**, watchmakers clamp a small magnifying glass into their eye to assemble tiny gear wheels. Stamp collectors, jewellers and doctors check details with a magnifying glass. At school and in nature, you can watch beetles and spiders in a bug viewer without hurting them. Smartphones also often offer a magnifier function using the camera.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lens that is thicker in the middle than at the edge and brings light together.
The point where a converging lens brings the rays of light together.
The bending of light when it passes from one substance into another.
A medieval magnifying glass that was laid on books.

gewusst: Even a drop of water on a leaf works like a small magnifying glass.
The German word for magnifying glass, Lupe, comes from the French “loupe”.

teile.einleitung: The lungs are the organ we breathe with. They take oxygen from the air into the blood and give off carbon dioxide again. Without our lungs we could survive for only a few minutes.
wichtigste: The lungs are the human organ of breathing.
They consist of two lungs in the chest.
In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood.
At the same time, carbon dioxide from the blood is breathed out.
The most important breathing muscle is the diaphragm.
The lungs contain hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs.
Smoking does serious harm to the lungs.

abschnitte.text: The lungs lie well protected in the **chest** behind the ribs. There are two **lungs**, a right one and a left one. The right lung has three lobes and the left only two, because the heart needs room there. The lungs are soft and spongy like a sponge. They are covered by a smooth, moist skin so that they can glide well when we breathe.

When you breathe in, air flows through the nose or mouth into the throat and then into the **windpipe**. The windpipe divides into two branches, the bronchi, which branch out finer and finer like the branches of a tree. At the ends there are tiny sacs, the **alveoli**. An adult has about 300 million of them. Spread out, they would cover an area of about 100 square metres, as much as a large flat.

The alveoli are surrounded by the finest blood vessels. **Oxygen** from the air passes through their wafer-thin walls into the blood. The heart then pumps the oxygen-rich blood around the whole body. In the other direction, the blood gives off **carbon dioxide** to the alveoli, and we breathe it out. This process is called gas exchange.

The lungs have no muscles of their own. The work is done mainly by the **diaphragm**, a flat muscle below the lungs. When it tightens, the space in the chest gets bigger and air flows in. At rest, adults breathe about 12 to 16 times a minute, and children a little more often. During sport we breathe faster and more deeply, because the muscles need more oxygen.

The lungs clean the air with mucus and fine hairs that carry dust upwards. Coughing helps to get rid of foreign bodies and mucus. **Smoking** damages the lungs very badly and can lead to lung cancer and other serious illnesses. In **asthma**, the bronchi narrow and breathing becomes difficult. Exercise in the fresh air and smoke-free rooms keep the lungs healthy, and the Swiss Lung League advises people with lung diseases.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchi, where oxygen passes into the blood.
The branches of the windpipe that distribute air in the lungs.
A flat muscle below the lungs that helps with breathing.
The passing of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of the blood.

gewusst: The left lung is a little smaller than the right, because the heart lies beside it.
A person breathes more than 10,000 litres of air in and out in a day.
The lungs of a healthy person contain so much air that a piece of lung tissue floats on water.

teile.einleitung: Ladybirds are small, round beetles, usually red or yellow with black spots. They are seen as lucky charms and are very popular with gardeners because they eat aphids. There are thousands of species worldwide.
wichtigste: Ladybirds like eating aphids best.
The number of spots does not show the age but the species.
The red colour warns enemies that the beetle tastes bad.
When in danger it gives off a yellow, bitter liquid.
Its wings for flying are hidden under the hard wing cases.
Ladybirds spend the winter hidden away, often in groups.
The harlequin ladybird is now common in Switzerland too.

abschnitte.text: Ladybirds have a body shaped like half a ball and are usually only a few millimetres long. Their hard **wing cases** are often red, yellow or black and have spots. The number of spots depends on the species and does not change during its life. The best known is the **seven-spot ladybird**, with seven black spots on a red background. Under the wing cases lie the thin, folded wings with which it flies.

Most ladybirds are predators and eat **aphids**. A single beetle can eat dozens of aphids a day. The larvae, which look like little grey crocodiles with spots, are also keen aphid hunters. Some species, on the other hand, eat fungal coatings such as mildew, or plants.

The bright colours are a **warning colour**, which signals to birds that the beetle is not good to eat. If a ladybird is threatened, it squeezes a yellow, bitter liquid out of its leg joints. This trick is called **reflex bleeding**. Ladybirds also often play dead and simply drop.

Ladybirds go through a complete **metamorphosis**. From the yellow eggs stuck to leaves hatch larvae, which shed their skin several times. Then they pupate on a leaf, and after about a week the adult beetle hatches. At first it is pale; the colours and spots only appear after a few hours.

In autumn, ladybirds look for sheltered hiding places, for example under bark, in fallen leaves or in cracks in walls. Often many beetles gather in one place. In a kind of winter rest they wait for spring. Sometimes they also spend the winter in houses, for example on window frames.

Many native ladybird species live in Switzerland. For several decades the **harlequin ladybird**, which was brought to Europe for pest control, has been spreading. It is very adaptable and partly pushes out native species. You can often recognise it by a black marking shaped like an M or W behind its head. By the way, the German name Marienkäfer goes back to the Virgin Mary, because the beetle was seen as a gift from heaven, and the English “lady” also refers to Our Lady.

begriffe.erklaerung: Hard front wings that protect the thin flying wings of beetles.
A striking colour that shows enemies that an animal is poisonous or not good to eat.
Giving off a bitter liquid from the leg joints for defence.
An animal that helps people, for example by eating pests.

gewusst: A ladybird larva can eat several hundred aphids while it is developing.
There are also ladybirds with 22 spots and ones with no spots at all.
In many countries it is considered lucky when a ladybird lands on your hand.

teile.einleitung: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place in all the world's oceans. It lies in the western Pacific near the island of Guam and at its deepest point reaches almost 11,000 metres down. If you stood Mount Everest in it, its summit would still be more than 2000 metres below the surface of the water.
wichtigste: The Mariana Trench is the deepest ocean trench on Earth.
Its deepest point is called the Challenger Deep and is almost 11,000 metres deep.
It lies in the Pacific east of the Mariana Islands, near Guam.
The deeper you dive, the greater the water pressure becomes.
In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh were the first people to reach the bottom.
In 2012 the film director James Cameron dived to the bottom alone.
Even at the bottom there are animals, for example small amphipods.

abschnitte.text: The Mariana Trench lies in the western **Pacific**, east of the Mariana Islands, whose largest island is **Guam**. It is about 2500 kilometres long but only about 70 kilometres wide, like a huge gorge in the sea floor. The deepest point is called the **Challenger Deep**, after the British research ship Challenger. Depending on the method, measurements give almost 11,000 metres.

The Earth's surface consists of large plates that move slowly. At the Mariana Trench, the **Pacific Plate** pushes under another plate and sinks into the Earth's interior. This process is called **subduction**. It causes earthquakes and volcanoes, from which the Mariana Islands have grown.

With every ten metres of water depth, the pressure rises by about as much as all the air above us presses on the Earth. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the **water pressure** is therefore over a thousand times as strong as on land. It is as if the weight of a car were resting on a thumbnail. On top of that it is completely dark down there and only a few degrees warm.

On 23 January 1960 the Swiss **Jacques Piccard** and the American Don Walsh became the first people to reach the bottom, in the bathyscaphe **Trieste**. The vessel had been developed by Jacques Piccard's father, Auguste Piccard. In 2012 the film director **James Cameron** dived down alone in the submersible Deepsea Challenger. In 2019 the American Victor Vescovo became the first person to reach the deepest points of all five oceans.

Despite the darkness, cold and pressure, there is life in the trench. At the bottom, small **amphipods**, sea cucumbers and bacteria have been found. A few thousand metres higher up there are still fish, such as the see-through snailfish. The animals feed mainly on scraps that slowly sink down from above.

Most of the deep sea is still hardly explored today. Researchers send robots and measuring instruments down to study rock, water and living things. Sadly, plastic rubbish has been found even in the Mariana Trench. Since 2009, part of the area has been designated a marine protected area by the USA.

abschnitte.titel: Childhood in a family of artists
abschnitte.text: Maria Sibylla Merian was born in 1647 in **Frankfurt am Main**. Her father was the well-known copper engraver Matthäus Merian the Elder, whose family came from **Basel**. He died when she was three. Her stepfather, the flower painter Jacob Marrel, taught her to paint. Even as a girl she collected caterpillars and painted them.

In Merian's time, many people believed that insects simply arise from mud or rotting things. Merian kept caterpillars in boxes at home and fed them with fresh leaves. In this way she saw how a caterpillar becomes a pupa and how a butterfly hatches from it. This change is called **metamorphosis**. In 1679 she published a book about caterpillars and their food plants.

Merian never painted the animals on their own, but always together with the plants they feed on. In one picture you often see the egg, caterpillar, pupa and butterfly on the same plant. In this way she showed the whole **life cycle** and the connections in nature. She made her pictures as **copper engravings**, which were then coloured by hand. They were both works of art and scientific illustrations.

Later Merian lived in **Amsterdam**, where she saw exotic insects in collections. In 1699, at the age of 52, she travelled with her daughter Dorothea to **Suriname** in South America. Such a journey was very unusual and dangerous for women at that time. For almost two years she watched and painted insects, spiders, frogs and plants there. An illness forced her to return in 1701.

In 1705 her famous book about the insects of Suriname was published, with 60 large plates. It made her known throughout Europe. Merian died in Amsterdam in 1717. Today she is considered a pioneer of **entomology**. In Germany she was pictured on the 500-mark note, and schools and a research ship also bear her name.

teile.einleitung: The cockchafer, also called the May bug, is a brown beetle that buzzes around trees in the evening in spring, especially in May. But it spends most of its life unseen as a larva in the soil. This larva is called a grub and lives in the ground for several years.
wichtigste: Cockchafers are seen especially often in May.
Their wing cases are brown, and their antennae look like little fans.
Adult cockchafers eat the leaves of trees.
The cockchafer's larva is called a grub and lives in the soil.
The grub eats roots and stays in the ground for several years.
A year in which especially many cockchafers fly in an area is called a flight year.
In central Europe there are mainly the common cockchafer and the forest cockchafer.

abschnitte.text: A cockchafer is about 2 to 3 centimetres long. Its **wing cases** are brown, and its head and the shield behind it are usually dark. On the sides of its abdomen it has white, triangular spots. Its **antennae**, which look like little fans, are especially striking; in males they are bigger. At the end of its body the beetle has a pointed extension.

Cockchafers live at the edges of woods, in orchards, parks and in meadows with trees nearby. The adult beetles eat the **leaves** of broadleaved trees such as oaks, beeches, maples and fruit trees. They fly mainly at dusk. After a few weeks they die.

The females lay their eggs in the **soil**. From them hatch fat, whitish, curved larvae, the **grubs**. They eat the roots of grasses, vegetables and trees and grow slowly. In Switzerland their development usually takes three years, and at higher altitudes four. Then they turn into a beetle in the soil, which crawls out in spring.

Because development takes the same length of time for almost all the animals in an area, the beetles there appear in large numbers only every three or four years. Such a year is called a **flight year**. In Switzerland, different flight-year areas are distinguished, such as the Bernese, the Uri and the Basel flight year. In years of mass outbreaks, cockchafers can strip trees almost bare.

In the past, cockchafers and their grubs caused great damage in farming. That is why in Switzerland and Germany the beetles were collected by schoolchildren and farmers, often for a small reward. In the 1950s and 1960s they were greatly reduced with **insecticides**, so that they became rare in many places. Today, organic farming uses among other things a **fungus** that attacks grubs.

The cockchafer is one of the best-known insects in the German-speaking world. It appears in old children's songs and plays a part in the story “Max and Moritz” by Wilhelm Busch, in which Uncle Fritz finds cockchafers in his bed. For a long time the cockchafer was also a popular motif on postcards and chocolate. In recent decades it has become more common again in some areas.
